chapters.title: The NetSuite Mental Model
chapters.subtitle: How the platform fits together

blocks.text: NetSuite is a cloud **ERP**: a single database that holds accounting, inventory, orders, customers, vendors, employees and more. Every business object (a customer, a sales order, an item) is a **record**.

You never touch that database directly. There is no SQL `UPDATE` and no direct table access. Every change goes through NetSuite's own APIs so that its business rules, permissions, sourcing and GL posting always run.
When something feels impossible, ask: which record holds this data, and which layer (configuration, workflow or script) is allowed to change it?

rows: Point-and-click setup: custom fields, forms, lists, roles
Shape the data model without code
JavaScript run by NetSuite on the server or in the browser
Business logic, automation, custom pages, APIs

blocks.text: Good NetSuite developers reach for these in order. Configuration is cheapest to maintain, workflows are next, and code is for everything the first two can't do cleanly.
External systems never connect to the database. They use **SuiteTalk** web services (REST or the older SOAP API) or a **RESTlet**, which is an HTTP endpoint you write yourself in SuiteScript.
The whole developer toolset (SuiteScript, SuiteTalk, SuiteFlow, SDF, the CLI) is branded **SuiteCloud**.
Before writing code, learn the product the way your users see it. Developers who skip this step write scripts that fight the platform.

items: **Show Internal IDs**: Home → Set Preferences → General → Show Internal IDs. Field IDs then appear when you hover or click a field label, and lists show record IDs.
**Global search**: the search bar accepts prefixes like `cus: acme` or `so: 1001` to jump straight to records.
**Record URLs**: a record's URL contains its internal ID, e.g. `.../salesord.nl?id=4512`.
**Customization menu**: Customization → Lists, Records & Fields; Customization → Scripting; Customization → Workflow.

blocks.text: Transactions flow into each other. Following one chain end to end teaches you more than any diagram:

items: **Sales Order**: the customer commits to buy. No GL impact yet.
**Item Fulfillment**: the warehouse ships. Inventory and COGS post.
**Invoice**: the customer is billed. Revenue and Accounts Receivable post.
**Customer Payment**: the money arrives and is applied to the invoice.

blocks.text: The mirror image on the buying side is **procure-to-pay**: Purchase Order → Item Receipt → Vendor Bill → Bill Payment.
Each downstream record links back to its source through the `createdfrom` field. Scripts and searches use it constantly.
Never experiment in **production**. Practice in a **sandbox** (a copy of production) or a **development account** (clean, no live data). Chapter 10 covers environments in depth.
Scripts and workflows in production can email customers, post to the general ledger and change inventory. Treat production like a live wire.

takeaways: NetSuite is one database of records; you change data only through NetSuite's APIs.
Customize in this order: configuration, then SuiteFlow, then SuiteScript.
External systems use SuiteTalk (REST/SOAP) or RESTlets you write.
Turn on Show Internal IDs on day one.
Order-to-cash: Sales Order → Item Fulfillment → Invoice → Customer Payment.

lab.title: Walk the order-to-cash chain
lab.goal: See how transactions link and learn your first field IDs.
steps: In a sandbox or dev account, turn on Show Internal IDs.
Create a customer. Note its internal ID from the URL.
Create a sales order for that customer with two item lines. Hover over Customer, Date and Memo and write down their field IDs (`entity`, `trandate`, `memo`).
Fulfill the order, then bill it to create an invoice.
Accept a customer payment against the invoice.
Open the invoice and find the Created From field. Click through back to the sales order.
On the sales order, open the Related Records subtab and identify every record in the chain.

flashcards.back: Any business object stored in NetSuite: customer, sales order, item, employee, custom record, and so on.
Configuration, SuiteFlow (workflows) and SuiteScript (code).
NetSuite's web services: the REST API and the older SOAP API.
An HTTP endpoint you write in SuiteScript for custom integrations.
The brand for NetSuite's whole developer platform and toolset.
Sales Order → Item Fulfillment → Invoice → Customer Payment.
Purchase Order → Item Receipt → Vendor Bill → Bill Payment.
The field that links a transaction to the transaction it was created from.

questions.q: How do external systems change data in NetSuite?
options: Through SuiteTalk web services or RESTlets
With direct SQL connections to the NetSuite database
By uploading files to the File Cabinet only
By editing the database through ODBC write access
questions.explain: NetSuite never exposes its database for writes. Integrations go through SuiteTalk (REST/SOAP) or RESTlets so business rules and permissions always apply.

questions.q: Which customization layer should you consider FIRST for a new requirement?
questions.explain: Configuration is the cheapest to build and maintain. Reach for workflows next and code last.

questions.q: Which transaction has NO general ledger impact?
questions.explain: A sales order is a commitment, not a financial event. Fulfillment posts inventory/COGS, the invoice posts revenue and A/R, and the payment posts cash.

questions.q: What is the correct order-to-cash sequence?
options: Sales Order → Item Fulfillment → Invoice → Customer Payment
Invoice → Sales Order → Item Fulfillment → Customer Payment
Sales Order → Invoice → Customer Payment → Item Fulfillment
Quote → Customer Payment → Sales Order → Invoice
questions.explain: Order, ship, bill, collect. (Some businesses bill before shipping, but this is the standard chain.)

questions.q: Which preference makes field IDs visible in the UI?
questions.explain: Home → Set Preferences → General → Show Internal IDs. It's the first thing every NetSuite developer turns on.

questions.q: What is SuiteCloud?
options: The brand for NetSuite's developer platform and tools
A paid add-on for extra storage
questions.explain: SuiteCloud covers SuiteScript, SuiteTalk, SuiteFlow, SDF and related tools.

questions.q: A downstream transaction points to its source transaction through which field?
questions.explain: `createdfrom` on an invoice or fulfillment holds the internal ID of the sales order it came from.

questions.q: What is a RESTlet?
options: A SuiteScript you write that is exposed as an HTTP endpoint
A workflow that runs on a schedule
questions.explain: RESTlets are custom endpoints. NetSuite's built-in REST API is SuiteTalk REST Web Services.

questions.q: Where should you practice writing scripts?
options: Any account, since scripts can't change data
questions.explain: Scripts can email customers and post to the ledger. Practice in a sandbox or development account.

questions.q: Which is the procure-to-pay sequence?
options: Purchase Order → Item Receipt → Vendor Bill → Bill Payment
Vendor Bill → Purchase Order → Item Receipt → Bill Payment
Purchase Order → Vendor Bill → Item Fulfillment → Customer Payment
questions.explain: Buy, receive, get billed, pay. It mirrors order-to-cash on the vendor side.

questions.q: Why can't you just run SQL UPDATE statements against NetSuite?
options: All changes must go through NetSuite's APIs so rules, permissions and postings run
NetSuite's database is read-only for everyone
SQL is only blocked in sandboxes
questions.explain: NetSuite enforces its business logic at the API layer. SuiteQL is read-only; writes always go through records.

questions.q: In the global search bar, what does typing `so: 1001` do?
questions.explain: Global search accepts record-type prefixes like `cus:`, `so:` and `inv:` to narrow results.

chapters.title: Records, Fields & IDs
chapters.subtitle: The data model every script touches

blocks.text: Every record has a **type** (like `salesorder`, `customer`, `inventoryitem`), an **internal ID** (a number, unique within that type) and **fields**.

items: **Body fields** live on the record header: `entity` (customer), `trandate`, `memo`, `status`.
**Sublists** are line tables. A sales order's `item` sublist has one row per product, with fields like `item`, `quantity`, `rate` and `amount`.
**Subrecords** are records nested inside a record, such as an address or inventory detail.

blocks.text: Scripts use **field IDs**, never the labels shown on screen. A label like "Customer" can be renamed per form, but its ID `entity` never changes.
Values also come in two flavors. `getValue` returns the stored value (for a list field, the internal ID of the selected option). `getText` returns what the user sees (the display name).

const custId = so.getValue({ fieldId: 'entity' }); // '342'
const custName = so.getText({ fieldId: 'entity' });  // 'Acme Corp'
Custom objects get script IDs with a prefix that tells you what they are. NetSuite adds the prefix for you; you choose the rest (e.g. `custbody_rush_order`).

rows: Field on a custom record type

blocks.text: Pick descriptive IDs up front. Renaming a script ID later breaks every script and search that uses it.

rows: Sales order, invoice, PO, item fulfillment, journal entry
Post to the GL and flow into each other

blocks.text: In code, record types are referenced with the `record.Type` enum, like `record.Type.SALES_ORDER` (value `'salesorder'`) or `record.Type.CUSTOMER`.
**Subsidiary**, **department**, **class** and **location** appear on almost every transaction and drive reporting.

In **OneWorld** (multi-subsidiary) accounts, subsidiary is critical: it sets the base currency and controls which entities and items can transact together. Many "why won't this save?" errors come from subsidiary mismatches.
**Sourcing** is NetSuite auto-filling fields from related records. Pick a customer on a sales order and terms, addresses, price level and sales rep fill in. Pick an item and the rate fills in.
Sourcing matters in scripts: it happens differently in standard and dynamic mode (Chapter 5), and setting fields in the wrong order can overwrite your values.
If you set `rate` and then set `item`, sourcing may replace your rate with the item's default price. Set the driving field first.

takeaways: Records have a type, an internal ID and fields: body fields, sublists and subrecords.
Scripts use field IDs, not labels. getValue returns IDs; getText returns display text.
Custom ID prefixes (custbody_, custcol_, custentity_, custitem_, custrecord_) tell you where a field lives.
Subsidiary, department, class and location classify transactions; subsidiary rules OneWorld.
Sourcing auto-fills fields from related records, so set driving fields first.

lab.title: Map a sales order
lab.goal: Document every important ID on one transaction.
steps: Open any sales order with Show Internal IDs on.
List 6 body fields with their IDs (start with `entity`, `trandate`, `memo`, `subsidiary`, `location`, `status`).
Open the Items subtab and list the sublist ID (`item`) and 5 line field IDs.
Find the shipping address and note that it is a subrecord.
Change the customer on a new order and watch which fields source in automatically.
Look up the sales order in the SuiteScript Records Browser (Help Center) and compare your list.

flashcards.back: Body fields are on the header (one value per record). Sublist fields are on line rows (one value per line).
getValue returns the stored value (an ID for list fields). getText returns the displayed text.
Custom transaction body field.
Custom transaction line (column) field.
Custom field on an entity (customer, vendor, employee...).
Script ID prefix for a custom record type.
Auto-filling fields from a related record, like terms from the customer.
Multi-subsidiary NetSuite; subsidiary drives currency and who can transact together.
A record nested inside another, like an address or inventory detail.

questions.q: A custom field with the ID `custcol_engraving` lives where?
questions.explain: `custcol_` means transaction column (line) field.

questions.q: Which prefix is used for a custom field on customer, vendor and employee records?
questions.explain: Entities share the `custentity_` prefix; you choose which entity types it applies to.

questions.q: What does this return for a sales order whose customer is 'Acme Corp' (internal ID 342)?
options: null, because entity is a list field
questions.explain: getValue returns the stored value. For list/record fields that's the internal ID. Use getText for the name.

questions.q: Why do scripts use field IDs instead of labels?
options: Labels can change per form or be renamed; IDs never change
Labels are only available in client scripts
IDs are shorter so scripts run faster
questions.explain: An admin can relabel "Customer" to "Client" on a form, but `entity` stays `entity`.

questions.q: On a sales order, `item`, `quantity` and `rate` on each product row are...
options: Sublist fields on the item sublist
questions.explain: The `item` sublist holds one row per product; those are its line fields.

questions.q: A shipping address on a transaction is an example of a...
questions.explain: Addresses and inventory detail are subrecords: records nested inside another record.

questions.q: In a OneWorld account, which classification controls base currency and which entities can transact together?
questions.explain: Subsidiary is the backbone of OneWorld. Mismatched subsidiaries are a classic save error.

questions.q: What is sourcing?
options: Auto-filling fields from a related record, like terms from the customer
Importing records from a CSV file
Loading script files from the File Cabinet
Copying a record to a new one
questions.explain: Selecting a customer sources terms, addresses and more; selecting an item sources its rate.

questions.q: A script sets `rate` to 50 and THEN sets `item`. The saved rate is the item's default price. Why?
options: Setting the item triggered sourcing, which overwrote the rate
Rate can't be set by scripts
Rates are always recalculated on save
questions.explain: Set the driving field (item) first, then override dependent fields (rate).

questions.q: What is the value of `record.Type.SALES_ORDER`?
questions.explain: The record.Type enum maps to lowercase record type IDs. (`SalesOrd` is the type value used in searches and SuiteQL.)

questions.q: Which prefix identifies a saved search?
questions.explain: Saved searches get `customsearch` script IDs; script records get `customscript`.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four standard classifications?
questions.explain: The classifications are subsidiary, department, class and location.

questions.q: Where can you look up every field ID for a standard record type?
options: The SuiteScript Records Browser in the Help Center
questions.explain: The Records Browser lists body fields, sublists, search columns and joins per record type.

chapters.title: Customization Without Code
chapters.subtitle: Fields, records, forms and roles

blocks.text: Before writing a line of code, ask: **can this be done with configuration?** Less code means fewer upgrade issues, no governance limits to worry about, and something an admin can maintain without you.
Custom fields add data to existing records. You create them under Customization → Lists, Records & Fields, choosing the kind (transaction body, transaction line, entity, item, CRM, other).

items: **Type**: free-form text, integer, decimal, currency, date, checkbox, list/record, multiple select, long text, rich text, hyperlink and more.
**Applies To**: which record types show it (e.g. Sale, Purchase, Customer).
**Source List / Source From**: pull a value from a related record automatically.
**Store Value**: checked means the value is saved. Unchecked means it is calculated or sourced each time it is shown and not stored.
**Default Value / Formula**: a default or a formula like `{quantity} * {rate}`.
**Display**: subtab, display type (normal, inline/read-only, hidden, disabled), mandatory.

blocks.text: Hidden fields are great for scripts that need to stash a value on a record without users seeing it.
A **custom list** (`customlist_`) is a simple set of dropdown values like Priority: Low / Medium / High. Point a List/Record field at it to give users a dropdown.
Use a custom record instead when each option needs more fields than a name.

A **custom record type** (`customrecord_`) is a brand-new table with its own fields (`custrecord_`), forms, permissions and searches. Use it for data NetSuite doesn't model: warranties, equipment, rebate agreements, integration logs.

items: **Parent-child**: on the child record, create a List/Record field pointing at the parent and check **Record is Parent**. The children then show as a sublist on the parent.
**Access**: control with permissions per role, or let anyone with the record type see it.
**Numbering**: optionally auto-number records, and choose whether to show a Name field.

blocks.text: An integration log as a custom record (request, response, status, timestamp) is one of the most useful things you'll ever build.
**Entry forms** (entities, items, custom records) and **transaction forms** control what users see: which fields and subtabs appear, layout, labels, and which fields are mandatory.
A transaction form can also attach a **client script** on its Custom Code tab, which is one way to run browser logic only on a specific form.
Hiding a field on a form doesn't secure it. Users may still see it through searches, other forms or exports. Use permissions for security.
Roles bundle permissions: which records you can view, create, edit or fully control, and which reports and setup pages you can open.

Scripts run in the context of a role too. A User Event runs as the user who triggered it, unless the deployment sets an **Execute As Role**. A large share of production bugs are really permission errors: works for the admin, fails for the clerk.
Test as a real end-user role, not as Administrator, before you call anything done.

takeaways: Always ask whether configuration can solve it before writing code.
Custom fields: choose type, Applies To, sourcing, Store Value and display settings carefully.
Custom lists are simple dropdowns; custom records are full tables.
Parent-child custom records use a List/Record field with Record is Parent checked.
Forms control layout, not security. Roles and permissions control security.

lab.title: Build a warranty tracker without code
lab.goal: Practice the configuration layer end to end.
steps: Create a custom list `customlist_warranty_type` with values Standard, Extended and Lifetime.
Create a custom record type `customrecord_warranty` with fields: customer (List/Record → Customer), type (List → your custom list), start date, end date.
Create a child custom record `customrecord_warranty_claim` with a List/Record field to the warranty and check Record is Parent.
Create a few warranties and claims. Confirm the claims sublist appears on the warranty.
Add a transaction body checkbox `custbody_rush_order` that applies to sales orders.
Create a custom sales order form that puts Rush Order at the top and makes it mandatory.
Log in with a non-admin role and confirm what it can and can't see.

flashcards.back: The field is calculated or sourced on display and not saved to the database.
A simple set of dropdown values (customlist_).
A new table with its own fields, forms, permissions and searches (customrecord_).
Checkbox on a List/Record field that shows child records as a sublist on the parent.
No. Forms control layout. Roles and permissions control security.
Deployment setting that makes a server script run with a specific role's permissions.
Read-only text on the form.

questions.q: Before writing a script for a new requirement, what should you ask?
options: Can this be done with configuration?
Which developer owns the File Cabinet?
questions.explain: Configuration is easier to maintain and avoids governance and upgrade issues.

questions.q: You need a dropdown of Low / Medium / High. What's the simplest tool?
questions.explain: Custom lists are made exactly for simple dropdown values.

questions.q: Each equipment unit needs a serial number, purchase date, location and owner. What should you build?
questions.explain: Data with several attributes of its own belongs in a custom record type.

questions.q: How do you make claim records show as a sublist on their warranty record?
options: Add a List/Record field on the claim pointing to the warranty and check Record is Parent
Add a sublist field on the warranty form
Create a saved search and attach it to the form
Write a User Event that copies claims onto the warranty
questions.explain: Record is Parent turns the child-to-parent link into a sublist on the parent.

questions.q: A custom field has Store Value unchecked. What happens?
options: The value is calculated or sourced when shown and isn't saved
The field is saved only on create
questions.explain: Unstored fields are display-time values, handy for showing sourced data without duplicating it.

questions.q: You hid the Credit Limit field on a form. Is the data now secure?
options: No; users may still see it through searches, other forms or exports
Yes; hidden fields can't be read anywhere
Yes, for all roles except Administrator
Only if Store Value is unchecked
questions.explain: Forms are layout. Use role permissions to secure data.

questions.q: A script works for the admin but fails for a warehouse clerk. Most likely cause?
options: The clerk's role lacks a permission the script needs
The script's API version is wrong
Client scripts don't run for non-admins
Governance limits are lower for non-admins
questions.explain: Scripts often run with the triggering user's permissions. Test with real roles, or use Execute As Role.

questions.q: Where can you attach a client script so it runs only on one specific transaction form?
questions.explain: Custom transaction forms have a Custom Code tab for attaching a client script.

questions.q: Which field type gives users a dropdown pointing at customers?
questions.explain: List/Record fields store an internal ID and display the selected record's name.

questions.q: Fields on a custom record type get which prefix?
questions.explain: `customrecord_` is the record type itself; its fields are `custrecord_`.

questions.q: What does the Execute As Role setting on a deployment do?
options: Runs the server script with that role's permissions
Restricts who can view the script record
Sets which role owns the script file
Limits the script to client-side execution
questions.explain: It lets a server script do things the triggering user's role can't, so grant it carefully.

questions.q: Which is a good use for a hidden custom field?
options: Letting a script store a value on a record that users don't need to see
questions.explain: Hidden fields are a handy scratchpad for automation. They are not a security feature.

chapters.title: Saved Searches & SuiteQL
chapters.subtitle: Querying NetSuite data

blocks.text: Saved searches are NetSuite's query builder and the single most useful skill to learn early. Admins use them for reports and dashboards; scripts use them to find records to process.

items: **Type**: Transaction, Customer, Item, a custom record, and so on.
**Criteria**: filters such as Type is Sales Order, Status is Pending Fulfillment, Main Line is true.
**Results**: the columns to return, optionally with a **summary type** (Group, Count, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Average).
**Available Filters**: filters users can change when they run the search.
**Audience**: who can see and run it.

blocks.text: Saved searches get script IDs starting with `customsearch` so scripts can load them by ID.
Transaction searches return **one row per line** by default: one for the header (the main line) plus rows for each item, tax and shipping line.

items: **Main Line = true**: one row per transaction (header only).
**Main Line = false**: only line rows, for line-level detail like item and quantity.

blocks.text: Duplicate rows in a transaction search almost always mean Main Line isn't set. Beginners hit this constantly.
Searches can reach into related records with **joins**. In a transaction search, the Customer fields join lets you show the customer's email or category.
**Formula** columns and criteria use SQL-like expressions with field IDs in braces:

CASE WHEN {amount} > 1000 THEN 'Big' ELSE 'Small' END
NVL({custbody_rush_order}, 'F')
TO_CHAR({trandate}, 'YYYY-MM')
{today} - {duedate}   -- days overdue
Group by a TO_CHAR({trandate}, 'YYYY-MM') formula and Sum the amount to get sales by month.
The `N/search` module creates or loads searches. Filters can be written as **filter expressions**: arrays joined by `'AND'` / `'OR'`.

items: `run().each()` stops after **4,000** results. Return `true` to keep going.
`run().getRange({ start, end })` returns at most **1,000** rows per call.
`runPaged({ pageSize })` handles large result sets: up to 1,000 rows per page.
`search.load({ id: 'customsearch_open_orders' })` loads an existing saved search.
`search.lookupFields()` reads a few fields from one record cheaply.

blocks.text: **SuiteQL** is a SQL dialect (based on SQL-92 / Oracle syntax) over NetSuite's analytics data source. It is **read-only** and great for joins that searches make awkward. Run it with `N/query` or the REST SuiteQL endpoint.

SELECT t.id, t.tranid,
       BUILTIN.DF(t.entity) AS customer,
       t.foreigntotal
FROM transaction t
WHERE t.type = 'SalesOrd'
  AND t.trandate >= ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, -1)

items: `BUILTIN.DF(field)` returns a field's display value instead of its ID.
Use `?` placeholders with `params` instead of string concatenation.
`runSuiteQL` returns up to 5,000 rows; use `runSuiteQLPaged` for more.
Transaction type values are codes like `SalesOrd`, `CustInvc`, `PurchOrd`.

blocks.text: Explore table and column names in the Records Catalog (Setup → Records Catalog).

takeaways: Saved searches have a type, criteria, result columns (with optional summaries) and an audience.
Set Main Line on transaction searches or you'll get one row per line.
Formulas use {fieldid} syntax with SQL functions like CASE, NVL and TO_CHAR.
run().each() caps at 4,000 results; use runPaged for more.
SuiteQL is read-only SQL over the analytics data source; use BUILTIN.DF for display values and ? params.

lab.title: Build four essential searches
lab.goal: Get fluent with criteria, results and summaries.
steps: Open sales orders by customer: Transaction search, Type = Sales Order, Status = Pending Fulfillment, Main Line = true. Results: Customer, Number, Date, Amount.
Overdue invoices: Type = Invoice, Status = Open, Main Line = true, Due Date before 30 days ago. Add a formula column `{today} - {duedate}` for days overdue.
Items below reorder point: Item search, criteria with a formula `{quantityavailable} < {reorderpoint}` (Formula (Numeric) = 1 using CASE).
Sales by month: Transaction search, Type = Invoice, Main Line = true. Results: formula TO_CHAR({trandate}, 'YYYY-MM') with summary Group and Amount with summary Sum.
Remove Main Line from search 1 and watch the duplicate rows appear. Put it back.
Rewrite search 1 as SuiteQL and run it in a SuiteQL tool or via N/query in the debugger.

flashcards.back: One row per transaction (the header line only).
Group, Count, Sum, Minimum, Maximum, Average.
4,000 results. Return true from the callback to continue.
1,000 rows per call.
SuiteQL function returning a field's display value instead of its internal ID.
Yes. It can only SELECT.

flashcards.front: Sales order type code in searches/SuiteQL
flashcards.back: SalesOrd
Cheap way to read a few field values from a single record.

questions.q: A transaction search shows each sales order 4 times. What's the most likely fix?
options: Add a Group summary to every column
Switch the search type to Customer
questions.explain: Without Main Line, transaction searches return the header plus every line.

questions.q: You want only line-level detail (item, quantity) from transactions. Which criteria?
questions.explain: Main Line = false excludes the header row and returns lines.

questions.q: How many results can `run().each()` iterate before it stops?
questions.explain: Use `runPaged()` for larger result sets.

questions.q: What's wrong with this callback?
options: It doesn't return true, so iteration stops after the first result
questions.explain: each() continues only while the callback returns true.

questions.q: What does `BUILTIN.DF(t.entity)` return in SuiteQL?
options: A boolean for whether entity is set
questions.explain: DF = display field. It converts an ID into its display text.

questions.q: Which statement about SuiteQL is true?
options: It can UPDATE records in bulk
It only works in client scripts
questions.explain: SuiteQL only queries. Writes go through records (N/record, REST, CSV import...).

questions.q: Which summary type would you use to total invoice amounts per customer?
options: Group on customer, Sum on amount
Count on customer, Group on amount
questions.explain: Group the dimension and Sum the measure.

questions.q: Which formula returns 'Big' when amount exceeds 1,000?
questions.explain: Saved search formulas use SQL CASE syntax with {fieldid} references.

questions.q: What's the safest way to pass a user-supplied value into SuiteQL?
options: A ? placeholder with the params array
questions.explain: Parameters avoid injection and quoting bugs.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of rows `getRange()` returns per call?
questions.explain: Request ranges of up to 1,000 at a time.

questions.q: Which is the cheapest way to read three field values from one known record?
questions.explain: lookupFields costs 1 unit and doesn't load the full record.

questions.q: Where can you browse SuiteQL table and column names?
questions.explain: Setup → Records Catalog documents records, fields and joins for SuiteQL.

questions.q: In SuiteQL, what `type` value identifies invoices in the transaction table?
questions.explain: Transaction type codes include SalesOrd, CustInvc, PurchOrd, VendBill, ItemShip.

questions.q: How many rows does `query.runSuiteQL` return at most?
questions.explain: Use `runSuiteQLPaged` beyond that.

chapters.title: SuiteScript 2.1 Basics
chapters.subtitle: Your first scripts

blocks.text: SuiteScript is JavaScript that NetSuite runs on its servers (or in the browser, for client scripts). Use **version 2.1**, which supports modern syntax: `const`/`let`, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring and more.
Version 1.0 (functions like `nlapiLoadRecord`) is legacy. You'll see it in old accounts but shouldn't write new 1.0 code.
Every file uses AMD-style `define()` plus JSDoc tags that tell NetSuite what it is.

items: `@NApiVersion 2.1`: the SuiteScript version.
`@NScriptType`: the script type (UserEventScript, ClientScript, ScheduledScript, MapReduceScript, Suitelet, Restlet...).
`define([...modules], callback)`: loads N/ modules and returns an object of **entry points**.
The returned keys (`beforeSubmit`) must match the entry point names for that script type.
**Upload the file** to the File Cabinet, usually under `SuiteScripts/`.
**Create the script record**: Customization → Scripting → Scripts → New, and pick the file. NetSuite reads the JSDoc tags.
**Create a deployment**: which record types it runs on, status (**Testing** or **Released**), log level, audience (roles) and Execute As Role.

blocks.text: Testing status runs the script only for its owner. Flip to Released when it's ready for everyone in the audience.
`log.debug(title, details)` writes to the deployment's **Execution Log** tab. Levels are debug, audit, error and emergency, and the deployment's Log Level setting filters what gets saved.

log.debug('Order loaded', { id: so.id, total: so.getValue('total') });
log.error('Failed to sync', e.message);
If your log.debug calls don't appear, check the deployment's Log Level. If it's set to Error, debug and audit entries are dropped.

items: Sublist lines are **zero-indexed** in 2.x.

blocks.text: **Standard mode** (the default) lets you set values in any order; sourcing and calculations happen on save. You set sublist values by line index with `setSublistValue`.
**Dynamic mode** (`isDynamic: true`) behaves like a user in the UI: fields source as you set them, so order matters. Sublists are edited one line at a time.
Use dynamic mode when you need sourced values (prices, tax, addresses) available before save, the way the UI shows them.
Wrap risky work in `try/catch` and throw meaningful errors with `N/error`. An uncaught error in beforeSubmit stops the save and shows the message to the user, which is exactly how you block bad data.

chapters.title: Script Types & Entry Points

sections.title: The script type decides when your code runs

blocks.text: Each script type has its own **entry points**: the function names NetSuite calls. You return them from `define()`.

rows: Server, when a record is loaded or saved
Validate or default on save, add buttons, create related records
Server, on a schedule or queued
Server, per record in a mass update

items: **beforeLoad(context)**: before the record is shown. Add buttons or fields with `context.form`, or set defaults on create.
**beforeSubmit(context)**: before the record is written. Change `context.newRecord` or throw to block the save. On create, the record has **no ID yet**.
**afterSubmit(context)**: after the record is committed. The ID exists; use it to create or update **other** records. Changing `newRecord` here does nothing.

blocks.text: `context.type` tells you the event: `CREATE`, `EDIT`, `DELETE`, `XEDIT` (inline edit or submitFields), `COPY`, `VIEW` and others. `context.oldRecord` holds the values before an edit.
A record saved by another User Event script does NOT trigger User Events. This prevents infinite loops but surprises people. Also, on XEDIT newRecord only contains the changed fields.
Client scripts run in the browser on a form. They get `context.currentRecord` (from N/currentRecord).

rows: Sourcing finishes after a field change
Before a field change is accepted
true to accept, false to reject
true to save, false to block

blocks.text: Client validation is convenience, not security. Imports, web services and other scripts bypass the browser. Enforce rules that matter in a User Event too.

items: Change the record being saved → **User Event beforeSubmit**.
Touch other records after a save → **User Event afterSubmit**.
Instant feedback while a user types → **Client script**.
Process a few hundred records nightly → **Scheduled**.
Process thousands of records → **Map/Reduce**.
A custom page or tool → **Suitelet**.
Another system needs to call NetSuite with custom logic → **RESTlet**.

blocks.text: If a script behaves differently from CSV imports or integrations, check `runtime.executionContext` and the deployment's execution context settings.

takeaways: User Event: beforeLoad (form), beforeSubmit (change or block the record), afterSubmit (touch other records).
On create, beforeSubmit has no ID yet; afterSubmit does.
Records saved by another User Event script don't trigger User Events.
Client validateField, validateLine and saveRecord must return true or false.
Client validation can be bypassed; enforce critical rules on the server.
Map/Reduce for volume, Scheduled for small batches, Suitelet for pages, RESTlet for APIs.

blocks.text: **Script parameters** (IDs start with `custscript_`) are fields on the script record whose values are set per deployment. Use them instead of hard-coding IDs, emails and thresholds.
Never hard-code secrets in a script. Store API keys as API Secrets (Setup → Company → API Secrets) or in a protected custom record, and use https.createSecretKey where supported.
Fields you add in Suitelets or beforeLoad must start with `custpage_`. They exist only on the page and aren't stored unless you save them somewhere yourself.
Don't build date strings by hand. Users have different date formats; N/format handles them.

Some modules only work in one place. `N/currentRecord`, `N/ui/dialog` and `N/ui/message` are client-side. `N/task`, `N/file` writes and `N/email` are server-side. Check each module's "Supported Script Types" in the Help Center.

chapters.title: Governance & Data at Scale
chapters.subtitle: Scheduled and Map/Reduce scripts

blocks.text: NetSuite is multi-tenant: your scripts share servers with other companies. So every execution gets a budget of **usage units**. Each API call costs units, and running out throws `SSS_USAGE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`.

rows: Client, User Event, Suitelet, Portlet, Workflow Action

blocks.text: There are also time limits and instruction-count limits, not just units.

items: `search.lookupFields`: 1 unit.
A search page / `run().each` / `runPaged().fetch`: about 5–10 units.
`query.runSuiteQL`: 10 units.
`email.send`: 20 units. `https.get/post`: 10 units. `task.submit`: 20 units.

blocks.text: Unit costs change between releases. Check the Help Center for current values.

items: Use `search.lookupFields` instead of loading a record to read a few values.
Use `submitFields` instead of load + save for body fields.
Never load records inside a loop when one search can fetch everything.
Move anything over a few hundred records into Map/Reduce.
Check `getRemainingUsage()` in long loops and stop gracefully.

blocks.text: A Scheduled script has one entry point, `execute(context)`. Deploy it on a schedule (daily, weekly, every 15 minutes...) or queue it with `N/task`. It gets 10,000 units and does **not** yield automatically.
Good for small nightly jobs. If volume might grow, write it as Map/Reduce from the start.

items: **getInputData()**: return the data to process: an array, an object, a search object or reference, or a SuiteQL query.
**map(context)**: called once per input item. `context.key` and `context.value` (a JSON string). Write key/value pairs with `context.write()`.
**reduce(context)**: called once per unique key written by map. `context.values` is an array of strings.
**summarize(summary)**: runs once at the end. Read errors and totals, send a report.
Map/Reduce **yields automatically** between invocations, so total volume isn't limited by one budget.
map and reduce invocations can run **in parallel** (concurrency is set on the deployment, limited by your processors).
You can skip map or reduce, but not both.
An error in one map call doesn't stop the others; read errors in summarize.

rows: One error can stop the run

takeaways: Every execution gets a unit budget; running out throws SSS_USAGE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.
Client/UE/Suitelet 1,000; RESTlet 5,000; Scheduled 10,000; Map/Reduce per stage.
Transactions cost most (load 10, save 20); lookupFields costs 1.
Don't load records in loops; use searches, lookupFields and submitFields.
Map/Reduce: getInputData → map → reduce → summarize; auto-yields and runs in parallel.
Read per-key errors in summarize via mapSummary.errors / reduceSummary.errors.

steps: Write a Scheduled script that loads every open invoice and sets a custom checkbox with load + save. Log remaining usage after each record.
Run it in a sandbox with lots of invoices and watch it hit SSS_USAGE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.
Rewrite it with submitFields and note how much further it gets.
Rewrite it as Map/Reduce: getInputData returns the search, map calls submitFields.
Add a summarize that logs usage, yields and any map errors.
Bonus: make reduce group open balance by customer and write it to a custom entity field.

questions.explain: RESTlets get 5,000.

chapters.title: Workflows, Suitelets & Integrations
chapters.subtitle: UI tools and talking to other systems

blocks.text: SuiteFlow is a visual **state machine** attached to a record type, built under Customization → Workflow.

items: **Initiation**: event-based (on create, on view or update) or scheduled, plus conditions.
**States**: e.g. Pending Approval → Approved → Rejected.
**Actions** inside states: set field value, send email, add button, lock record, create record, show message, or run a Workflow Action script.
**Triggers** decide when actions run: Entry, Exit, Before Record Load, Before Record Submit, After Record Submit, Scheduled.
**Transitions** move between states, triggered by events, buttons or conditions.

blocks.text: Use workflows for approvals and simple field logic that admins should be able to maintain. Use SuiteScript for heavy logic, loops over lines, external calls or anything performance-sensitive.
A Workflow Action script (entry point `onAction`) lets a workflow call code for the one step it can't do itself, and its return value can be stored in a workflow field.
A Suitelet answers HTTP requests at its own URL with `onRequest(context)`. Build pages with `N/ui/serverWidget` or write raw HTML.
GET shows the form; POST handles the submit. Form field values arrive in `context.request.parameters`.

rows: Standard REST API for records plus a SuiteQL endpoint
Custom logic, many operations in one call, custom payloads

items: `get` and `delete` receive URL parameters; `post` and `put` receive the request body.
With `Content-Type: application/json`, the body arrives already parsed and returned objects are serialized.
URL: `https://<account>.restlets.api.netsuite.com/app/site/hosting/restlet.nl?script=123&deploy=1`.
RESTlets get 5,000 units per call.

blocks.text:
GET https://<ACCOUNT_ID>.suitetalk.api.netsuite.com/services/rest/record/v1/customer/123

POST https://<ACCOUNT_ID>.suitetalk.api.netsuite.com/services/rest/query/v1/suiteql
Prefer: transient
{ "q": "SELECT id, companyname FROM customer WHERE isinactive = 'F'" }
The record service supports GET, POST (create), PATCH (update), PUT (upsert by external ID) and DELETE. Sandbox account IDs use a hyphen in URLs, like `1234567-sb1`.

items: **Token-Based Authentication (TBA)**: OAuth 1.0a signed requests. An **Integration record** provides the consumer key/secret; an **access token** (tied to a user and role) provides the token ID/secret. Requests are signed with HMAC-SHA256.
**OAuth 2.0**: authorization code flow, or machine-to-machine client credentials using a certificate.
Plain username/password login for web services is no longer supported.

blocks.text: Turn on the features under Setup → Company → Enable Features → SuiteCloud (REST Web Services, Token-Based Authentication, OAuth 2.0).
The integration's role decides what it can do. Give it only the permissions it needs, and never use an Administrator token for an integration.

takeaways: SuiteFlow is a state machine: initiation, states, actions with triggers, transitions.
Workflows for approvals and simple logic; scripts for heavy or performance-sensitive logic.
Suitelets: onRequest; GET renders, POST processes; fields come from request.parameters.
RESTlets: get/delete take params, post/put take the body; 5,000 units.
SuiteTalk REST is the default for new integrations; SuiteQL has its own endpoint.
Authenticate with TBA (OAuth 1.0a) or OAuth 2.0, using a least-privilege role.

options: When you need custom logic or several operations in a single call
Whenever you need to read a customer
questions.explain: RESTlets shine for custom payloads and business logic.

questions.q: In this RESTlet call, what is `params.id`?
options: The value of the id URL parameter
questions.explain: get receives the URL query parameters as an object.
questions.code:
// GET .../restlet.nl?script=123&deploy=1&id=42
const get = (params) => search.lookupFields({ type: 'customer', id: params.id, columns: ['email'] });

questions.q: Which workflow trigger runs actions just before the record is saved?
questions.explain: Like a User Event's beforeSubmit, but configured visually.

questions.q: How do sandbox account IDs appear in SuiteTalk URLs?
options: As a separate sandbox domain only
questions.explain: The account ID 1234567_SB1 becomes 1234567-sb1 in the hostname.

chapters.title: SDF, Environments & Deployment
chapters.subtitle: Working like a professional

blocks.text: The **SuiteCloud Development Framework (SDF)** lets you keep scripts **and** configuration (custom fields, records, workflows, searches, deployments) in files, in Git, instead of clicking them into each account by hand.

my-project/
  src/
    manifest.xml        # project type, dependencies
    deploy.xml          # what to deploy
    FileCabinet/
      SuiteScripts/     # your .js files
    Objects/            # XML: customscript_*, custbody_*, customrecord_*...

items: **Account Customization Project (ACP)**: for your own company's account. The usual choice.
**SuiteApp project**: a packaged app (with an ID like `com.mycompany.myapp`) distributed to other accounts, often through the SuiteApp Marketplace.

blocks.text: The older way to move customizations between accounts is **Bundles** (SuiteBundler). You'll still see them in many companies.

npm i -g @oracle/suitecloud-cli

suitecloud project:create -i         # new project (interactive)
suitecloud account:setup             # authenticate to an account
suitecloud object:import             # pull existing objects as XML
suitecloud file:import               # pull File Cabinet files
suitecloud project:validate --server # check before deploying
suitecloud project:deploy            # push to the account
There are also SuiteCloud extensions for VS Code and WebStorm that wrap the same commands.
Run `project:validate --server` before every deploy. It catches missing dependencies and bad references against the real account.
`@oracle/suitecloud-unit-testing` adds Jest with stubs for the N/ modules, so you can test script logic without an account.

rows: The live business. Don't experiment here.
A copy of production (data + config) refreshed on request. Account ID has a suffix like 1234567_SB1. Email can be redirected.
Temporary account to test your customizations against the next release before it hits production.
A clean account without production data, for building SuiteApps or practicing.

blocks.text: NetSuite ships **two major releases a year**. Use Release Preview to catch anything an upgrade breaks before your users do.
A sandbox refresh overwrites the sandbox with a fresh copy of production. Anything built only in the sandbox is lost, which is another reason to keep work in SDF and Git.

items: Develop locally in an SDF project, committed to Git.
Deploy to a sandbox with `suitecloud project:deploy`.
Test with deployments in **Testing** status and real end-user roles.
Get sign-off, then deploy the same project to production.
Flip deployments to **Released** and watch the Execution Log.

blocks.text: Keep account-specific values (internal IDs, emails) in script parameters so the same code works in sandbox and production.

takeaways: SDF keeps scripts and configuration objects in files you can version in Git.
ACP for your own account; SuiteApp projects for distributed apps; Bundles are the legacy route.
CLI: project:create, account:setup, object:import, project:validate --server, project:deploy.
Unit test with @oracle/suitecloud-unit-testing (Jest + N/ stubs).
Production, sandbox (_SB1), Release Preview and development accounts each have a job.
Flow: SDF + Git → sandbox → test in Testing status → production → Released.

lab.title: Put your account under version control
steps: Install Node.js and the SuiteCloud CLI.
Run `suitecloud project:create -i` and create an Account Customization Project.
Run `suitecloud account:setup` against your sandbox or dev account.
Import the scripts and custom objects you built in earlier chapters with object:import and file:import.
Commit everything to a Git repo.
Change a script, run `project:validate --server`, then `project:deploy`.
Add one Jest unit test with @oracle/suitecloud-unit-testing and run it.

questions.q: What does SDF let you do?
options: Manage scripts and configuration objects as files in version control
questions.explain: Customizations become XML and JS files you can review, diff and deploy.

questions.q: Which project type do you use for your own company's account?
questions.explain: SuiteApp projects are for packaged apps distributed to other accounts.

questions.q: Where do custom field and script deployment definitions live in an SDF project?
options: In the Objects folder as XML
questions.explain: Objects/ holds XML for custom objects; FileCabinet/ holds files.

questions.q: Which command checks your project against the real account before deploying?
questions.explain: Server validation catches missing dependencies and bad references.

questions.q: Which command pulls existing custom objects from an account into your project?
questions.explain: file:import does the same for File Cabinet files.

questions.q: What is a sandbox account?
options: A copy of production that you can refresh on request
A blank account with no data
questions.explain: Sandboxes carry production data and configuration, with a suffix like _SB1.

questions.q: What happens to work built only in a sandbox when it's refreshed?
options: It's overwritten by the fresh copy of production
questions.explain: Keep work in SDF and Git so a refresh doesn't erase it.

questions.q: What is a Release Preview account for?
options: Testing your customizations against the next NetSuite release
Previewing a script before saving it
questions.explain: NetSuite ships two major releases a year; Release Preview lets you test early.

questions.q: Which package adds Jest with N/ module stubs?
questions.explain: It lets you unit test script logic without an account.

questions.q: What's the healthiest order of steps?
options: SDF + Git → sandbox → test in Testing status → production → Released
Edit in production, then copy to sandbox
Deploy to production in Released status, then test
questions.explain: Test in a safe environment first, with real roles, then release.

questions.q: How do you keep the same code working in sandbox and production when internal IDs differ?
options: Put account-specific values in script parameters
Hard-code both and check the URL
questions.explain: Parameters are set per deployment, so each account gets its own values.

questions.q: What is the legacy way to move customizations between accounts?
questions.explain: Bundles are still common, but SDF is the modern approach.

questions.q: How many major NetSuite releases ship per year?
questions.explain: Use Release Preview each time to catch regressions.
